bloques: Intenseflow is an open-source source port of id Software's classic first-person shooters Wolfenstein 3D and Spear of Destiny to the cross-platform multimedia library Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL2). It is meant to keep the original feel while taking advantage of some improvements mentioned in the list below.

Intenseflow is the successor of Wolf4SDL, which was written by Moritz "Ripper" Kroll. It was renamed because the code base has changed a lot since the last Wolf4SDL release. The name is an anagram of "Wolfenstein".
The game data files are not part of Intenseflow. You need your own copy of Wolfenstein 3D and/or Spear of Destiny, the shareware versions work as well.
Cross-platform: Linux, BSD variants, macOS and Windows (MinGW). The continuous integration builds on Linux, macOS and Windows (MSYS2). Only little endian platforms like x86 and ARM are supported.
One binary for all game versions: The version of the game is detected at runtime from the data files that are found. There is no need to build a separate binary for each version.
AdLib sounds and music: This port includes the Nuked OPL3 emulator (Nuked-OPL3-fast), so you can hear the AdLib sounds and music without any AdLib-compatible sound card in near to perfect quality.
Multichannel digitized sounds: Digitized sounds play on 8 channels, so in a fire fight you will always hear when a guard opens the door behind you.

Higher screen resolutions: Aside from the original 320x200 resolution, any multiple of 320x200 is supported, the default being 640x400. Other resolutions of at least 320x200 can be forced, which may result in graphic errors. Intenseflow does not apply any bilinear or similar filtering, so the graphics are not blurred but pixelated just as we love it.

Fully playable with only a game controller: Intenseflow can be played completely without a keyboard. At least two buttons are required (shoot/YES and open door/NO), but five or more are recommended (run, strafe, ESC).
Two additional view sizes: One view size uses the full width of the screen and shows the status bar, like in Mac-enstein, and one view size fills the whole screen (press TAB to see the status bar).
(Nearly) unlimited sound and song lengths: Mod developers are not restricted to 64kB for digitized sounds and IMF songs, so longer songs and digitized sounds with better quality are possible.
Resuming ingame music: When you come back to the game from the menu or load a save game, the music is resumed where it was suspended.

Freely movable pushwalls: Moving pushwalls can be viewed from all sides, allowing mod developers to place them with fewer restrictions. The player can also follow the pushwall directly instead of waiting until it has left a whole tile.

Optional integrated features for mod developers: Shading, directional 3D sprites, floor and ceiling textures, high resolution textures and sprites, parallax sky, cloud sky and outside atmosphere (star sky, rain, snow). They are disabled by default and are enabled with CMake options, see Building.

bloques: A native PC port of a GameCube fighting game (disc ID GRSEAF), produced by static recompilation rather than emulation: the disc's PowerPC executable is translated ahead of time into C, compiled for x86-64, and run as native code inside a Dolphin-derived runtime that provides the graphics, audio, input and hardware emulation around it.
No game data and no game code are distributed here. You supply a disc image you already own; setup extracts it and recompiles it on your machine.

This is still early. Expect rough edges: the game is playable start to finish, but features arrive before their polish does, and something that worked last release can break in the next one. Polish is planned throughout rather than saved up for a 1.0 — and bug reports genuinely help, because most of what gets fixed here was found by someone hitting it.

Fully playable — boots to menu and through gameplay. Every block of the game's own executable runs as native code; the recompiler translates 535,368 instructions with 0 unknown opcodes and no interpreter fallback inside them.

What the interpreter does still cover is the PowerPC exception vectors — 0x500 (external interrupt), 0xC00 (system call), 0x800 (FP unavailable). Those handlers are written into low RAM by the OS at boot rather than living in the disc's executable, so there is no recompiled code to dispatch to and the interpreter runs them until control returns. They account for about 0.7% of executed steps, steadily, because interrupts fire for the life of the session — but only 0.2% of cycles, so there is nothing to win by recompiling them. Rendering is Vulkan on the GPU, with the CPU emulation and the runtime on separate cores.

Screenshots taken in Super Odyssey PC Recomp at 3840 x 2160 (click for full size). The game is © Nintendo; you need your own copy to run it.

All three console exclusives in one game: Spawn, Link and Heihachi. Soulcalibur II came out on the Xbox with Spawn, on the GameCube with Link and on the PlayStation 2 with Heihachi, and none of those releases had more than one of them. This port has all three on the same select screen, in every mode, against each other.

An unofficial native port of Soulcalibur II (Xbox) for macOS, Linux (Steam Deck and Steam Machine included), Windows and Android. It is a static recompilation of the Xbox game: its program is translated ahead of time into C and runs on a native runtime, with no emulator. It adds a training mode, online play with rollback, a free camera with a pause, widescreen, higher resolutions and shaders.

No game files are included. Your own Soulcalibur II Xbox disc image is the only one you need to play: the USA disc, or the European one (Europe, Australia), which plays in English, German, French, Spanish or Italian (the Language feature; on macOS, Windows and Linux, not yet Android). Link and Heihachi are optional: give the launcher your own GameCube disc, PlayStation 2 disc, or both, to add them. This project cannot help you get any of them.

The Xbox game has Spawn. Link and Heihachi are converted on your machine from your GameCube and PlayStation 2 discs (models, moves, weapons, voices, select-screen art and endings) and stand beside him: in Arcade, VS, the Extra modes, Weapon Master, and the Museum's profiles, theaters and Art Gallery.

Hit boxes (the game's own collision shapes: where each fighter can be hit, and its weapon and limbs, red while an attack is live), frame data (startup, active, recovery, advantage on hit or guard) with a frame meter, an input display and a combo readout down each fighter's side, start over (the round as it began, one key), a dummy that records and replays what you show it (in Practice or VS Battle), health refill and infinite time; with save states, pause and frame advance, and slow motion from the in-game menu. See docs/PLAYING.md.

Two players, each on their own machine. Host from the launcher or from the in-game menu while you play, and give the other player the match's code (or find each other in the lobby, or invite them from the launcher's waiting room); join with the code. Fights use rollback; the menus wait for both players. During a match: both players' names, the ping, and a chat (T). A dropped connection waits for the other player to come back with the same code. See docs/online.md.

Switched on in the launcher: \ (backquote) or a click of the right stick takes the game's camera and flies it, in fights and menus. P (or Start while flying) pauses the fight while the camera goes on flying; . (or White) steps a frame; H (or Black) hides the life bars and timer; F12 saves a screenshot.
Widescreen (the game's own 16:9 mode) and resolutions up to 8x (5120x3840).
HD textures: the GameCube version's HD texture pack for Dolphin, from your own download, matched to the Xbox's textures when you import it; or dump the game's textures and make your own.
Shaders: RetroArch's CRT and scanline shaders (CRT Royale, CRT Guest, CRT Lottes and more) at the Xbox's 480 lines, or your own preset.
An endless battle: in any fight, the game plays both fighters for as long as you like (touch the controls to take one over).
An in-game menu (Esc, F1 or a gamepad's Back): save states, speed, training, cheats (no damage, one-hit knockouts, everything unlocked), online, sound, quit.

Android: the launcher and the game in one app for 64-bit phones and tablets (Android 10 or later, Vulkan), with touch controls (a stick, the four attack buttons, Start and the menu) beside any gamepad.

Static recompilation of Super Mario World (SNES) into native C, using the snesrecomp framework. This repo is the per-game side: the runtime, the recompiled C output, the per-game .cfg, and the build glue.

The 65816 CPU code from the ROM is statically translated to C — every function the game runs on the SNES's main CPU is a real generated C function in src/gen/. The rest of the SNES is not recompiled — it's hardware. PPU rendering, the APU / SPC700 audio coprocessor, DMA and HDMA channels, hardware register I/O, and bank-mapping all run through a C reimplementation of the SNES hardware in snesrecomp/runner/src/snes/ — a LakeSnes-derived core (the same emulator family the snesrev reverse-engineered ports use), with individual algorithms credited to snes9x. Runs the PS4 The Last of Us Remastered (CUSA00552, with its update 1.11) natively on Windows. The game's own x86-64 code runs directly on the PC; a runtime supplies the PS4 system libraries, and a Vulkan renderer (the shadPS4 video core) executes the PS4 GPU work.

No game files are in this repository. You need your own copy of the game (the dumped CUSA00552 folder, and its update). This project is not affiliated with Sony Interactive Entertainment or Naughty Dog.
Why The Last Of Us Remastered (PS4 version) is superior to The Last Of Us Part I (remake)?
The PS4 remaster preserves the artistic style of the PS3 version and just improves the resolution and graphics.
Last version with multiplayer support, having multiplayer code is much easier to implement community/unofficial multiplayer
Use less resources and storage space (no 4K textures, less polygons, no ray-tracing) than the remake version, which has a history of performance problems and poor optimization on PC.
Work in progress, reported playable from start to finish by a player, with one crash along the way that is not fixed yet (a workaround is under Known issues), and with rough edges.

Frame rate: on a laptop with a Core i7-8750H and a GTX 1050 Ti Mobile (4 GB), 60 FPS in light areas and about 40-44 FPS in the heaviest area tested, where the CPU side of the renderer is the limit (the draw recording thread at about 87%): lowering the resolution barely helps there.
Frame pacing: frame times swing while the game runs below its limit, and a fixed 30 FPS limit (launcher, or the in-game menu) makes motion clearly more even.

NPCs moving in jumps or bobbing up and down (GitHub #57, #63): the game read some results of its GPU memory copy shader (Cs_MemCpy) a frame late. They are read back now; in a save where they jumped every time, they stopped. Tested on one save and one GPU so far: report it if they still jump somewhere (GOW3_TLOU_MEMCPY_READBACK=0 turns the fix off for comparison). Thanks to KyrieFrost, whose experimental patch in #63 pointed at that shader.

A frame that compiles many new shaders can pause the game for a moment, mostly the first time an area is played. The game's own frame watchdog is patched from 2 s to 20 s for that (TLOU_FIXES=none leaves the game unpatched). If a load ever hangs, start with GOW3_FRAMES_IN_FLIGHT=0 (slower).

Pistol and rifle shots that went through scenery with no effect (firefly pendants that could not be shot down, GitHub #29, #45; walls that took no bullet holes from a pistol or rifle while a shotgun marked them) are fixed. The game asks the GPU, with an occlusion query, whether a character is under the crosshair; while one is, the player's bullets ignore scenery so thin cover in front of a target does not stop them. The runtime made up the answers to occlusion queries (always "visible"), so the bullets ignored scenery all the time; the queries are now real Vulkan occlusion queries…

On NVIDIA graphics cards older than Turing (GTX 900 and 10 series), the game's cloth solver for its largest cloths (Cs_ClothSimulate512) lost the Vulkan device in Pittsburgh, once Henry and Sam appear: the runtime stopped with Device lost during submit, and Windows' System event log shows nvlddmkm "SKEDCHECK19_CTA_REGISTER_CONSUMPTION failed". A replay of that route lost it on 17 of 18 runs, on drivers 582.53 and 582.78, whatever was changed in the shader. Its one workgroup of 512 threads needs all the registers of a multiprocessor; on those cards it now runs as 256 threads that simulate 2…

make compiles every binary's code, reads the data its sources declare from your disc, and checks each binary it rebuilds against the original, PRS compression and all. They land under build/, at the disc's own paths. make checks 1ST_READ.BIN, LOADER.BIN and each file it reads from SONICADV/ against SHA256SUMS before reading it. This is a matching build, so an edit that changes a byte of output fails it.

make check needs no disc. It compiles the sources it can check without the disc, using placeholders for imported data where needed, and checks each linked source against its recorded hash, but builds no complete binary. Checks says what each goal shows, and make help lists them all.

make dc builds the sources with GCC 16.2 and links every image anew, under build/dc/ at the disc's paths. It needs the disc but neither SHC nor wibo. Its first run builds binutils and GCC from source (Toolchain); their logs are in build/toolchain/. make dc-disc needs the disc's .gdi and its tracks in orig/, not its files alone. The port's features describes what it adds.

make dc-check needs neither disc nor SHC. It builds the port's disc-independent objects and writes build/dc/check.txt: hashes of those objects, SH4ZAM's archive, the toolchain's libgcc.a and two compression results. Compare the file across hosts at the same commit, with the same SH_ELF (Checks). Its first run builds the toolchain and fetches SH4ZAM, as make dc does.

make pc builds the game from your disc, and make play runs it in a window. The engine's build goals need Python 3.9 or later; a window needs SDL3 and Vulkan. Checks lists the other host requirements, and Build goals lists the engine's commands.
Dedicated to my good friend and mentor, Julien.

Super Mario Odyssey (version 1.0.0) running natively on Android, built on the static recompilation from smo-recomp.

And no, it's not an emulator. No CPU interpreter, no JIT, no compatibility layer. The game's ARM64 code gets translated to C ahead of time and compiled for Android with the NDK, and this project's runtime takes care of the rest: the console's system libraries, NVN graphics (on Vulkan), shaders, audio, input and the file system.
There's no game code, no game assets, no keys and no firmware in this repo. You need your own copy of the game and keys dumped from your own console.

Made with AI. Most of the code was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant (through Claude Code), with the project's creator directing it, reviewing it and testing it on a real phone. Expect some rough edges, and if something breaks, please send logs (see below).
The game boots, plays and saves! Here's how it runs on the two phones we've measured, both on the phone's own driver:
Galaxy S24 Ultra (the dev's phone, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 / Adreno 750): about 58–60 fps in Cascade at 100% scale, up from about 44 in beta 0.2.
Xiaomi 2406APNFAG (u/CAPELINI_W's phone, MediaTek Dimensity 8300 / Mali-G615 MC6): about 40 fps, fairly stable, at handheld resolution, with no graphical issues. A 30 fps limit holds steady.

Your results will likely be different. Speed depends a lot on the phone's chip, its GPU driver, how warm it gets and your settings. Other phones are untested, so we'd love to hear how yours does. Custom drivers are optional. The first start builds the graphics for your phone, which takes a few minutes, but only once (and again after an update that changes the shaders).
Import your own game right in the app: your prod.keys, then your NSP or XCI of 1.0.0 (base game, no update). The keys stay in the app's private storage until you remove them.
Steady game speed: the game keeps its normal speed even below 60 fps. FPS limit from 20 to 60.
Save export and import as a .zip (your current save is kept as a backup).
RomFS mods you can turn on and off in the app.
Docked (1080p) or handheld (720p) resolution, scale presets, or your own resolution scale.
Upscalers (bilinear, bicubic and more) for any scale under 100%.
FPS counter and performance overlay (average fps, 1% low, frame time).
Uses your phone's own Vulkan driver by default. On Snapdragon you can also load custom AdrenoTools driver packages (like Mesa Turnip).
On-screen touch controls with Switch-style button icons, plus a layout editor to move and resize every button and stick.
Any controller Android sees as a gamepad, with button rebinding in the app.

The house button on the touch controls (or the controller's Home button, rebindable) opens the in-game menu: change settings while the game is paused, restart, or exit. Exit waits for any save in progress, then takes you back to the app's menu.

Every 10 seconds the log notes the fps, 1% low, CPU clocks, heat, and where each frame's time went (GPU, game logic, shader building), so a slowdown or a stutter on your phone can be tracked down. No saves, keys or game files in there.

This recompilation is a byproduct of developing snesrecomp — the games are the proving ground, the framework is the goal. Static recompilation of The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past (SNES) into native C, using the snesrecomp framework. This repo is the per-game side: the runtime, the recompiled C output, the per-game .cfg, and the build glue.

The 65816 CPU code from the ROM is statically translated to C — every function the game runs on the SNES's main CPU is a real generated C function in src/gen/. The rest of the SNES is not recompiled — it's hardware. PPU rendering, the APU/SPC700 audio coprocessor, DMA and HDMA channels, hardware register I/O, and bank-mapping all run through an embedded copy of snes9x's emulator core (snesrecomp/runner/snes9x-core/). Same model as N64Recomp and similar projects: recompile the CPU, emulate the silicon.
The ROM is never redistributed — you supply your own legally-dumped copy.

The game is all you need to play. The Nightly release is the latest work in progress, rebuilt overnight whenever something's changed; the numbered releases are the ones to play.

The Mac app isn't notarized, so the first time, run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/ALTTP-DX.app or allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security. On Linux, chmod +x the AppImage first. On Windows, SmartScreen asks once: "More info", then "Run anyway". Put the game somewhere you can write to, so it can update itself.

From v1.8 on, you download the game by hand once. When the start menu opens, it asks GitHub in the background whether there's a newer version, and if there is, an Update button shows up under the title. Nothing downloads until you press it. The game checks the download against the size and SHA-256 GitHub publishes, puts it in place and restarts:
Mac: the whole ALTTP-DX.app is swapped for the new one. A file the game downloads itself isn't quarantined, so xattr is a one-time thing.
Linux: the AppImage is replaced in place, under the same name, so your shortcuts keep working.
Windows: the files beside zelda3.exe are replaced, except your zelda3.ini.

Your saves and settings carry over. Under General, Check For Updates turns this off, and Update Channel picks Releases or Nightly. The start menu's bottom-right corner says which version you're on, and a build you made yourself never offers to update. The tools are still a download of their own. From a terminal, --version prints the version, --check-update releases asks without changing anything, and --update releases (or nightly) does the whole thing.

A static recompilation of Sonic Adventure (Dreamcast, US v1.005) to the Sony PSP. It is not an emulator. The game's SH-4 executable and its code overlays are translated ahead of time into C, one C function per SH-4 function, and compiled with psp-gcc. The Katana SDK layer the game calls into (Shinobi, Ninja, KAMUI, the sound driver) is replaced by native PSP code: sceGu for graphics, sceAudio for sound, sceIo for files. No PowerVR, AICA or ARM7 is emulated.

Disclaimer. This is vibecoded: AI coding agents (Claude) wrote practically all of it; the author steered, play-tested on real hardware and made the calls. Expect AI-written code: verbose, uneven, sometimes over-engineered. Judge it on whether it runs, not on whether it's pretty. One thing that isn't slop: the testing. Recorded input tapes replay the game frame-for-frame, and every change had to keep them identical, plus picture comparisons and runs on the real PSP. So whatever the code looks like, the game behaves like the original.
The original design document (plan, hardware gap, architecture, milestones, risks) is docs/design.md. Code and reports cite it as "README §N"; those section numbers refer to that file.
What works, on a PSP-3001 with ARK-4 CFW:
The whole of Sonic's story runs: all 44 tested places (levels, acts, adventure fields, bosses) start and play.
Saving works (the VMU save becomes a Memory Stick file, docs/vmu.md).
Audio works: ADX music and voices, and the sequenced sound effects played from the game's own sound banks (docs/m3-audio-report.md).
Station Square runs at full speed: ~31.5 ms per game frame against the 33.3 ms budget for 30 fps.
Heavy stages run at full game speed with frame skip. Game logic keeps real time and pictures are dropped. Emerald Coast needs ~61 ms to draw a frame, so it shows about 9 pictures a second.

Speed in heavy stages and bosses. Logic alone is over budget in a few places, e.g. Sky Deck 3 (~38.5 ms) and Windy Valley 2 (~39 ms); Chaos 0 and Casino 2 sit at about 30-31 ms. The per-place numbers are in devkit/surveys/stage-survey.md and devkit/surveys/fskip-survey.md.

Texture memory on the card is tighter than under PSPLink. An EBOOT started from the Memory Stick gets about 4 MB less user memory than the same code loaded as a PRX through PSPLink. At boot the largest free block is 7680 KB against 11776 KB, so the texture pool gets 6 chunks instead of
The rest of the blur and dropped detail comes from this. Best lead: ARK-4's high-memory option (devkit/tx2/capacity-notes.md). To mimic the card under PSPLink, pass --tex-chunks 6.
Media Engine. The second CPU runs our code, but every Media Engine run hangs the next PSPLink reboot, so it is unused (branch me-wip). Only probe it with someone at hand to power-cycle the PSP.
PSP replays are not yet deterministic, so tapes are checked bit-for-bit on the desktop only.
tools/psp_run.py stages a PRX only when its size or date differs. A newer build of the same size can be skipped silently, so touch the PRX before a run. The proper fix is to compare content.
Game data: bring your own disc
There is no SEGA data in this repository: no disc files, no recompiled game code, no SDK material. tools/check_clean.py (pre-commit hook and CI) refuses anything that looks like game data.
You need your own GD-ROM dump of Sonic Adventure US v1.005. Every address in recomp/ is specific to that version.
Do not ask for game files or dumps in issues. Such requests will be closed.
No prebuilt EBOOTs are provided. The EBOOT contains the recompiled game code, so you build your own from your own dump.

bloques: A native Windows x64 version of Super Mario Odyssey (1.4.1), made by static recompilation of the Nintendo Switch game, with its own runtime and a Vulkan renderer.

It is not an emulator: there is no CPU interpreter and no JIT, and no console firmware runs. The game's AArch64 machine code is translated to C ahead of time and compiled for the PC; the system libraries, graphics API, audio, video, input and file system the game uses are re-implemented by this project's runtime.

This repository contains no game code, no game assets, no keys and no firmware. You need your own copy of the game, dumped from your own console. The build reads the dump's decrypted files: no keys and no firmware are needed. Everything derived from the game is generated on your PC, under build/, and never leaves it.

Import. scripts/setup.py reads your decrypted dump in place and converts the program's modules to ELF.
Function list. Every function of the executable, with boundaries from its own unwind tables and symbols (54,214 in main).

Lifting. tools/lifter/recomp.py turns each AArch64 function into a C function; clang compiles them into a game DLL. A differential test runs sampled instructions both lifted and in the Unicorn emulator: 23,194 of 23,194 equal.

Runtime. runtime/ stands in for the console: threads with the console's three-core scheduling, files and journalled saves, NVN graphics on Vulkan with a Maxwell shader translator, the audio renderer, controllers, movies, Help and the offline system services.

This is a complete decompilation of the GameCube debug build of Resident Evil 4, G4BE08, the "Nov 25 2004" prototype on two discs. The debug build shipped with Bio4.sym symbol files that name every function, and that is what made a full decompilation possible.

Building the repository gives back the exact original files: main.dol and all 114 REL overlays, checked against config/G4BE08/build.sha1 on every build. The source is about 570,000 lines of C and C++ in src/ and 44,000 lines of headers in include/, with no assembly files.
The code is built with the compilers the original was built with:
There are no game assets in this repository. To build it you need your own images of the debug discs. Disc 1 has main.dol and most of the RELs, disc 2 has the four RELs for the island stages.
You need Linux, Python 3 and ninja. The first configure run downloads decomp-toolkit, objdiff, wibo and the CodeWarrior compilers. The SN GCC is built once from SN's source:
ninja finishes with a progress report that should say 100% matched and linked. To check the result, build/tools/dtk shasum -c config/G4BE08/build.sha1 should print one OK per file, 115 in all.
When working on one unit, python3 tools/bytecmp.py game/foo compares its object file with the original, and python3 tools/fdiff.py game/foo shows one function side by side.

src/game/ is the game itself. src/em*/ are the enemies, src/wep*/ the weapons, src/pl*/ the player characters and src/st*/ the rooms, one REL per room. src/t_*/, src/Tools/ and src/tools/ are the in-game debug editors, src/Sscrn/ the menu screens and src/lib/ the SDK, CRI and runtime libraries.
include/ has the headers, including the reconstructed structs.
config/G4BE08/ has the unit lists, symbols, splits, linker scripts and per-REL data.
tools/ has the build scripts, the compare tools, the SN compiler build and the research kit. tools/motion_export.py exports the game's animations to glTF and BVH, see tools/motion/README.md.
docs/overview.md is a guide to how the engine fits together. docs/matching.md explains how the matching was done and docs/unit-notes.md has notes per unit. docs/research/ is the detailed log.

Every unit compiles to the original bytes with the original compilers. In some places the compiler only picks the same registers or instruction order as the original if the code is written in a particular way, and no natural way of writing it was found. Those spots are marked with a // COMPILER-DIFF: comment, 526 of them at the moment. Most are a dead test, an empty asm("") or a register T x asm("rN") declaration. None of them puts an instruction into the output, and python3 tools/asmcheck.py --all checks that. docs/matching.md explains the reason behind each kind. Getting this number down is…

Almost all the assembly left is code the original developers also wrote in assembly, because their compilers couldn't express it in C. That's the paired-single math and matrix routines, the GQR setup, an exception handler, the cache and SPR code in the CRI video decoder, and eight startup, debugger and decompression units that were assembly to begin with. In the game code asmcheck.py counts 231 instructions of it, with the eight assembly units counted separately. The exceptions are in the CRI libraries: one small block in dct_ac that works around a difference between our build of CodeWarrior…

Function names are Capcom's own, from Bio4.sym. They are C++ mangled names, which is why the game code is C++ and the SDK, CRI and C library code is C. File names and the split into units come from the D:/Bio4/Prog/ .cpp paths the asserts left in the binaries.
This is a reverse engineered clone of Zelda 3 - A Link to the Past.
It's around 70-80kLOC of C code, and reimplements all parts of the original game. The game is playable from start to end.
You need a copy of the ROM to extract game resources (levels, images). Then once that's done, the ROM is no longer needed.

I got much assistance from spannerism's Zelda 3 JP disassembly and the other ones that documented loads of function names and variables.

This disassembly was created with a number of specific guidelines:
Top-level labels use a mix of PascalCase and snake_case, where underscores will separate arbitrary hierarchies, such as Sprite_MoveFunction. Sublabels use pure snake_case.

The beginning of every line will have an address marker of the form |AAAAAA|, where AAAAAA is the 24-bit address in ROM in hexadecimal. APU source will have :SSSS following the ROM address, where SSSS is the 16-bit hexadecimal address once transfered to the SPC.
Code or data that appears unreachable is labelled UNREACHABLE_AAAAAA.
Unreachable blocks of the filler byte $FF are labelled with NULL_AAAAAA and given a comment with FREE ROM: .
For data bank and direct page changes, the full address will be written out.
In data tables, the number of entries per line is determined by how they should logically be grouped. In all other cases, they are grouped in sets of four or eight.
A list of standardized names for various entity classes is found in values.asm.
Some comments have [WORD] annotations to categorize them.

A Pomeranian walks into post-apocalyptic Tokyo. No, seriously.

Tokyo Jungle (2012) is the most wonderfully absurd game Sony ever published — a survival action game where you play as animals fighting for dominance in a Tokyo abandoned by humanity. One moment you're a tiny Pomeranian sneaking past lions in Shibuya, the next you're a dinosaur asserting territorial control over Yoyogi Park. It's brutal. It's beautiful. It has no business being as good as it is.

Tokyo Jungle was a PS3 exclusive. The Western release was digital-only — no disc, no physical backup. Both of its developers are gone (Japan Studio dissolved 2021, Crispy's dormant since 2015). The PS3 store is running on fumes. Sony's PS Plus cloud streaming for PS3 titles has been broken for months. Nobody is coming to save this game.

Tokyo Jungle Recompiled is a native PC port built using ps3recomp — a static recompilation toolchain that translates PS3 PowerPC binaries into native C code, then compiles them as x86-64 executables. No emulation at runtime. No compatibility layers. Just raw, recompiled native code.
Status: Phase 8 — Boots to a Window, Audio Initialises, Geometry Not Yet Drawing

This is the first 3D title to attempt ps3recomp. The game boots end-to-end, opens a D3D12 window, runs its PSN data-install flow, brings up SPURS and all twelve of its SPU job images, loads its game data, and completes audio initialisation. Its own clear colour reaches the screen. It no longer hangs, crashes or exits — it now parks in its main loop waiting on a single counter that nothing in the emulator writes. It does not yet draw geometry.

A note on the function count. Earlier builds advertised 35,208 lifted functions. That number was wrong, and the current one is lower on purpose: find_functions was treating intra-function basic blocks as separate function entries, inventing tens of thousands of phantoms. It now covers those blocks properly. The fix was checked against ground truth on a different title that ships an unstripped debug build (+90 real functions recovered, 0 phantoms introduced) — Tokyo Jungle's own binary is stripped, so its count cannot be verified directly. The honest figure is 7,924. A count going down was…
7,924 PPU functions recompiled to native C++ and compiled to x86-64
A window with the game's own pixels in it — CELL_GCM CLEAR_SURFACE reaches the D3D12 backend and presents; the frame colour is the guest's, not ours

The PS3 data-install flow — the title's installer runs to completion, which needed all three of ps3recomp's independent path roots configured (sys_fs syscalls, the cellFs HLE prefix table, and cellGame's content path)
Guest threads actually run — ppu_install_thread_trampoline; without it every sys_ppu_thread_create thread spawned, reported FINISHED, and executed nothing
SPURS job chains — the walker handles JOB / SYNC / NEXT / GUARD, and job guards are implemented, so a chain waits for its notify instead of running against parameters the game has not filled in yet

All 12 SPU images lifted and dispatched — captured with SPU_DUMP_MISS, matched by content fingerprint, 4,751 SPU functions, zero dispatch misses. The sound jobs run to completion, read their work descriptors and DMA their results
Every file the boot asks for opens — the disc, hdd-game and app_home roots all resolve into the title's real data (input/USRDIR/, 1,053 files); the sound banks load. Zero failed opens across a run

You'll need the assembler, Asar v1.91 (you can find it here).
Click the big green "Clone or download" button and select zip file.

On Linux, steps are the same but use asar instead of asar.exe and PATCH.sh instead of PATCH.bat.
All 5 versions assemble and play exactly like they should!
Anyone can contribute as long as they follow the format rules below. This isn't like a personal project or anything. Just make sure every commit that the ROM will properly assemble.
mikeyk for the original disassembly this one was based off of from 2013.
@loveemu for the original disassembly of the SPC700 sound engine code.
reformatting the original disassembly into an assemblable project via Asar.
creating labels and descriptions for RAM addresses.
documentation on all versions other than the U version, and including their differences in the project.
pulling data like graphics, palettes, and level data out of the text files and into binary files.
extracting constants and magic numbers from code and turning them into assembler variables.
All contributors, which can be found on the GitHub page for this repo.
I'm focusing on readability so its important that everything is nice and consistent. This has, can, and will change in the future.
Labels on their own lines. 4 spaces per indentation in code. Inline comments on column 46.

Address mode hints (.B .W .L) should be used by the following instructions if they are not accumulator addressed: TSB TRB BIT LDA LDX LDY STA STX STY STZ CMP CPX CPY ORA AND EOR ADC SBC ASL ROL LSR ROR DEC INC. Some address modes (e.g. LDA $addr,Y) are unambiguous but should be kept for consistency.
Everything should be relative, using labels. This is kind of assumed, but it is very important with multiple version support since stuff shifts around a lot.
Any operand that refers to an address should use a variable. This includes immediates.
Large datablocks should be placed in bin files and incbin'd in the disassembly, to reduce text file size.
Data of certain formats should be separated in a commonly editable format (e.g. palettes as \*.pal files instead of SNES 15-bit data).
Version differences should be clearly marked with special comments. See label GameMode17 in bank_00.asm.
Exceptions are single instructions with either different addressing modes (use the applicable macro) or different constant operands (use the con function).
Constants and magic numbers should be pulled out into an assembler define.
If a constant is used as a bitmask, it should be written in binary.

Don't allow variable names to be a prefix of another variable's name. This way you can Ctrl+F a variable name and you won't get similarly named variables. (This is why scratch RAM starts with an underscore.) Generally this means short names are bad.
Probably more things that I'll add as I think of them.

This is a fully commented and documented, reassemblable disassembly of the US release of Final Fantasy for the NES. Everything you need to reassemble is included.
This can be used for whatever means you want, but the goal was for it to allow for a ridiculous easy way to perform ASM hacks and bugfixes to the game.

Final Fantasy has numerous bugs. As I was going through this disassembly, I uncovered several. I tried to label them all with "BUGGED". So if you do a "find in files" for that, you will be able to see most of them. I try to get into detail of how they're bugged and usually offer a suggested fix.
The *.asm files are pretty self explanatory. However there are a few other files:

build.bat is a batch file to generate a ROM from the source. So just make your changes to the asm, run build.bat, and your hack is done! NOTE that build.bat will delete any "bank_*.bin" and "*.o" files in the root directory as part of its cleanup.

macros.inc includes a handful of macros that are [sparesely] used. Really the main ones are the CRITPAGECHECK and PAGECHECK which error/warning if a timed loop (branch) crosses a page boundary, as this would screw with the timing of the routine (crossing a page adds another cycle)

Constants.inc includes various constants. Should be self explanitory mostly. I tried to keep the number of addresses listed in there to a minimum. The ones that are in there are primarily for addresses that point somewhere in the middle of a block of binary data, so it's hard to create them with labels.
variables.inc is the closest thing to a RAM map that I have. It's not really as organized as it could be, and some of the names are questionable, but hopefully get the point across well enough.

"some formats.txt" is some very sketchy notes I made about some less-than-obvious formats used by the game. Specifically tile attributes for overworld and standard maps, and the battle formation data. This is a holdover from when I started this project. As I got further into it, I started putting these descriptions in large block comments in the actual code -- since that seemed to make more sense and was more organized.
As mentioned, since work for this has spread over several years, my style may be inconsistent in parts. Sorry! I like to think I improved as time went on.

For large blocks of data that's intermingled in the code, I've been trying to put those into seperate binary files and .INCBIN'ing them. The /bin/ directory has them. The naming is a little inconsistent, but one thing to note is that if they have an address in them ("0D_storytext_A800.bin" for example) then they include a pointer table at the start.
Anyway that's about it. A lot of this isn't polished yet, as I was going to go over everything and clean it up/make it prettier once I finished all the commenting.

You need a copy of the ROM to extract game resources (levels, images). Then once that's done, the ROM is no longer needed.
It uses the PPU and DSP implementation from LakeSnes, but with lots of speed optimizations.

You must self-build for now. Super Mario All-Stars Launcher for Super Mario World
This is a simple launcher for the Super Mario All-Stars branch of the Super Mario World port by snesrev. It allows you to easily run the game on your system.
Note: The releases and source code are updated in tandem. Please choose the option that suits you best, as both options provide the same functionality.
Before using this launcher, make sure you have the following installed:
Option 1: Using the Executable (Simpler and Cleaner)
Executable versions for Mac and Linux will be forthcoming.
Go to the "Releases" section of the repository.
Create a new folder and place the downloaded executable in it.
Copy the Super Mario All-Stars ROM (smas.sfc) and Super Mario World ROM (smw.sfc) into the same folder.
The launcher will launch the game, and you can start playing.
Option 2: Using Python (Recommended for Python users)
Python has tentative support for Mac and Linux.
Note: During the installation of Python make sure to check the box that adds Python to PATH.
Download the source code from the repository.
Create a new folder and place the downloaded source code in it.
Copy the Super Mario All-Stars ROM (smas.sfc) and Super Mario World ROM (smw.sfc) into the same folder.
On Windows run the "Install-Dependencies-for-Windows.bat" file to download the required Python packages.
On Mac or Linux run the "Install-Dependencies-for-Mac-and-Linux.sh" file to download the required Python packages.
After downloading the dependencies, run the "launcher.pyw" script on windows or "Run on Mac and Linux.sh" on Mac and Linux.
The launcher will install the needed backend and then launch the game, and you can start playing.
If you encounter any issues while using the launcher, please refer to the repository's issue tracker for known problems and solutions. You can also report new issues to help improve the launcher.

This is a port of the AlephOne engine to Android. Yes, this means you can now play the Marathon saga on your Android phone! :robot: You can even play online!

Download the APK of the desired chapter from the releases page from your phone and install it. Your phone may complain about the APKs signature as it is not registered with the Google Play Store, simply ignore the warnings. Enjoy!
The game supports playing with a bluetooth keyboard and/or a bluetooth joystick (such as a PS4 controller). In both cases you can configure your input from the preferences screen.
If you want you can also play using touch controls. There are no on-screen controls for now, here's how they work:
You can find some options in the preferences to tune your touch experience by adjusting dead zones and the virtual stick size.
The game supports playing scenarios but you have to do a bit of work by following these instructions:
Place a file called AlephOneScenario.txt in the root of your phone's storage.
Place the scenario you want to play somewhere on your phone.

Write the path to the root folder of the scenario as the first line of AlephOneScenario.txt, such as /sdcard/Evil. If you are not sure what your path is, try /sdcard/Your Scenario Folder or /mnt/sdcard/Your Scenario Folder

Make sure the AlephOne you are going to use is authorized to access storage. Considering that the app is not signed some phones will deny access to storage without asking. Check in your phone's settings.
Run any of the games (M1/M2/MI), the scenario should run instead.

At the moment be sure to put your scenarios in your phone's memory. Putting them on an SD card will probably not work because the app has no write access to the SD card. This maybe confusing because the path to your phone's internal storage will probably still be /sdcard. Don't worry about that.
Save games for the scenario will be placed inside the scenario's folder and will be separate from the main game(s).
If you want to go back to playing the bundled game you don't need to delete the AlephOneScenario.txt file, you can simply put a # in front of the scenario path to disable it, such as: #/sdcard/Evil.

Source code to Super Mario World (SNES disassembly)
This was my first large-scale reverse engineering project. It assembles the binary exact ROM Super Mario World (U) [!].smc.
An older modified version of WLA is used to assemble the code. A modified tool that can handle all graphic formats is provided, but sadly I have lost the source code.
This project is being archived for historical purposes, as-is, and I do not intend to continue it.
Extract the archive located in the bin folder. Run wla.bat in the root and follow the instructions. It simplifies the need to manually type out a bunch of shit in the command line.
